sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: We introduce OvisOCR3, a 0.8B model for a broad range of OCR-related tasks. OvisOCR3 unifies document parsing, general OCR, key information extraction (KIE), document figure captioning, and cross-page table reconstruction in a single model. We train the model on real and synthetic data through continued pretraining and use domain-balanced mid-training to balance supervision across tasks with different data volumes and response lengths. Multi-teacher on-policy distillation transfers expertise from five domain-specific 4B teachers into the shared model, followed by mixed-task reinforcement learning with domain-specific rewards. We compare OvisOCR3 with general-purpose vision-language models and specialized OCR models on public and in-house benchmarks covering all five task families. In these comparisons, it achieves an overall score of 96.74 on OmniDocBench v1.6 and the highest overall scores on PureDocBench, Real5-OmniDocBench, and MDPBench. On OCRBench v2, it ranks first, scoring 65.9 and 61.3 on the English and Chinese splits, respectively. It also outperforms the baselines on OCRBench and all four KIE benchmarks. On DocFigCapBench, it achieves the highest localization F1 and a caption score close to that of Qwen3.8-Max. For cross-page tables, it leads in Relation F1 on CrossTabBench and truncated-table TEDS on MPDocBench-Parse. These results demonstrate that a compact 0.8B model can achieve strong performance across diverse OCR-related tasks. OvisOCR3 is available at https://huggingface.co/ATH-MaaS/OvisOCR3.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Optical character recognition (OCR) converts text in images into machine-readable content. In practical applications, however, accurate transcription is only starting point. Users may need the structure of an entire page, an answer to question about its content, or set of fields extracted according to specified schema [1, 2]. Figures can carry information absent from the surrounding text, while tables spanning multiple pages must be recovered as complete structures [3]. These requirements call for models that combine accurate reading with taskdirected understanding and structured generation, producing representations suited to different downstream needs. Our previous work, OvisOCR2 [4], demonstrated that compact 0.8B end-to-end model can achieve leading document parsing performance through carefully designed data and posttraining. Extending this approach beyond page parsing is not simply matter of adding more tasks to the training mixture. Different OCR tasks vary substantially in response length and in what constitutes correct output. full-page reconstruction can contain thousands of tokens, whereas field extraction may require only few; balanced sample counts therefore do not ensure balanced supervision under token-averaged loss. Moreover, accurate transcription, informative figure descriptions, and correct cross-page table associations require different forms of supervision and feedback. The challenge is to achieve specialist-level performance across broader range of tasks with compact model. We introduce OvisOCR3, 0.8B model that unifies document parsing, general OCR, key information extraction, document figure captioning, and cross-page table reconstruction. Our goal is to achieve leading performance across these tasks while retaining single compact model for deployment. Built on Qwen3.5-0.8B [5], OvisOCR3 performs each task according to the supplied instructions and shares the same parameters across all five domains. Continued pretraining on real and synthetic data builds common foundation for the five domains. During domain-balanced mid-training, we rebalance the task mixture and train two branches with token-level and sample-level loss normalization. We fuse their weights at the end of this stage. Multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) then integrates expertise from five domain-specific 4B teachers into the shared student. Finally, mixed-task reinforcement learning (MixRL) jointly refines the model with domain-specific rewards. The teachers are used only during training; inference requires no separate task-specific models. We evaluate OvisOCR3 on public and in-house benchmarks covering all five task families. In document parsing, it achieves an overall score of 96.74 on OmniDocBench v1.6 and the highest overall scores among the compared models on PureDocBench, Real5-OmniDocBench, and MDPBench. It also leads our comparisons on OCRBench, both language splits of OCRBench v2, and all four KIE benchmarks. On DocFigCapBench, OvisOCR3 achieves the highest localization F1 among the compared models and caption score close to that of Qwen3.8-Max, leading specialized OCR models on both metrics. For cross-page tables, it achieves the highest relation F1 on CrossTabBench and the highest truncated-table TEDS on MPDocBench-Parse. These results demonstrate that broad OCR task coverage and strong task-specific performance can be combined in single 0.8B model.

sections.title: 2 Model Capabilities
sections.content: The capabilities of OvisOCR3 span text recognition and localization, document structure recovery, and visual content understanding. We organize them into five task families according to their prediction targets and output representations  (Table 1)  . These families operate at different 2 levels of granularity, from individual text regions to complete pages and tables spanning multiple pages. All five share the same model parameters, with task-specific instructions defining the information to be recovered and its representation. Table 1: Task coverage and output representations of OvisOCR3.

sections.title: General OCR
sections.content: Key information extraction Document figure captioning Cross-page table reconstruction Recovery of page content, layout, and reading order Recognition, localization, translation, and visual reasoning Extraction and organization of fields from images Localization and description of document figures Continuation detection and table reconstruction across pages Region-level JSON or Markdown with LaTeX and HTML Transcriptions, bounding boxes, LaTeX, chart data, labels, or answers Key-value records or template-guided JSON Localized captions and Mermaid representations HTML tables with source-page associations, or no-continuation prediction Tasks involving localization use common spatial representation: bounding boxes are specified by their upper-left and lower-right corners, with horizontal and vertical coordinates normalized to integers in 0999 relative to the input image width and height, respectively.

sections.title: 2.1 Document Parsing
sections.content: Document parsing aims to recover the content and spatial organization of page from its image. While OvisOCR2 supports only Markdown document parsing, OvisOCR3 introduces two additional capabilities: structured document parsing and document layout detection. Beyond expanding task coverage, OvisOCR3 further improves parsing quality, especially for multilingual documents and photographed pages.

sections.title: 2.1.1 Structured Document Parsing
sections.content:
Structured parsing represents page as JSON array of region-level records in reading order. Each record associates bounding box (bbox) with category from predefined taxonomy (category) and the corresponding region content (content). The content representation depends on the region category: text uses Markdown, mathematical expressions use LaTeX, and tables use HTML. Images and charts are referenced by HTML image tags whose paths encode their bounding boxes. Prompt Analyze the document structure and extract text content. Return single JSON array in natural reading order. Each element follows this schema: `{"bbox": [x_min, y_min, x_max, y_max], "category": "string", "content": "string"}` Rules: 1. The bbox coordinates are integers scaled to [0, 1000). 2. The category is exactly one of: 3 Prompt (continued) ["abstract", "algorithm", "aside_text", "chart", "content", "display_formula", "doc_title", "figure_title", "footer", "footer_image", "footnote", "formula_number", "header", "header_image", "image", "inline_formula", "number", "paragraph_title", "reference_content", "seal", "table", "text", "vertical_text", "vision_footnote"]. 3. The content formatting depends on category: - For "footer_image", "header_image", "image", or "chart": write as an HTML image tag . - For "display_formula" or "inline_formula": write in LaTeX. - For "table": write as standard HTML `...
`. - Otherwise: write in Markdown. 4. Output must be strictly valid JSON. Properly escape quotes and special characters inside content.

sections.title: 2.1.2 Document Layout Detection
sections.content: Document layout detection predicts the locations, semantic categories, and reading order of page regions without transcribing their content. Its output consists of JSON records containing bbox and category fields. This formulation shares the coordinate convention and category taxonomy of structured parsing but omits the content field. Prompt Analyze the document structure and return single JSON array in natural reading order. Each element follows this schema: `{"bbox": [x_min, y_min, x_max, y_max], "category": "string"}` Rules: 1. The bbox coordinates are integers scaled to [0, 1000). 2. The category is exactly one of: ["abstract", "algorithm", "aside_text", "chart", "content", "display_formula", "doc_title", "figure_title", "footer", "footer_image", "footnote", "formula_number", "header", "header_image", "image", "inline_formula", "number", "paragraph_title", "reference_content", "seal", "table", "text", "vertical_text", "vision_footnote"].

sections.title: 2.1.3 Markdown Document Parsing
sections.content:
Markdown document parsing converts page image into single Markdown document in reading order, preserving the source text without translation or paraphrasing. Mathematical expressions and tables are represented in LaTeX and HTML, respectively, while images and charts are referenced by coordinate-bearing HTML image tags. Unlike structured parsing, this formulation represents page content as continuous document rather than sequence of regionlevel JSON records, without assigning explicit bounding boxes or category labels to individual text regions. Prompt Extract all readable content from the image in natural human reading order and output the result as single Markdown document. For charts or images, represent them using an HTML image tag: , where left, top, right, bottom are bounding box coordinates scaled to [0, 1000). Format formulas as LaTeX. Format tables as HTML: ...
. Transcribe all other text as standard Markdown. Preserve the original text without translation or paraphrasing.

sections.title: 2.2 General OCR
sections.content: General OCR covers ten tasks spanning text recognition and localization, structured content extraction, translation, and visual understanding. The task formulations differ in both the information supplied with the image and the prediction target, supporting outputs ranging from plain text and spatial coordinates to structured data, category labels, and answers. Table 2 summarizes these interfaces. Table 2: The ten General OCR interfaces. Every task receives an image; the second column lists additional task inputs. Bounding boxes use the order [xmin, ymin, xmax, ymax], with integer coordinates normalized independently by image width and height to [0, 1000).

sections.title: 2.2.1 Plain OCR
sections.content: Plain OCR transcribes all readable text from scanned pages, screenshots, signs, handwritten notes, or text crops. It preserves the original wording, language, and reading order, using spaces and line breaks rather than document markup or bounding boxes. Prompt Read all the text in the image. Directly output the content. Rules: 1. Preserve the original text exactly without translation, paraphrasing, correction, or completion. 2. Follow the natural human reading order. 3. Output plain text only. Use spaces and line breaks only to preserve text separation and reading order. 4. Do not output Markdown, HTML, JSON, bounding boxes, category labels, explanations, or code fences.

sections.title: 2.2.2 Word-Level Text Spotting
sections.content: Word-level text spotting jointly localizes and transcribes each readable word or text token in an image. It returns JSON array in reading order, with each record pairing transcription with bounding box that tightly encloses the corresponding word or token. 5 Prompt Locate and transcribe every readable word or text token in the image. Return single JSON array in natural reading order. Each element follows this schema: `{"bbox": [x_min, y_min, x_max, y_max], "text": "string"}` Rules: 1. Use word-level annotations. Each element must represent exactly one visible word or text token. Do not merge multiple words into text line, paragraph, label, or table cell. 2. The bbox coordinates are integers scaled to [0, 1000). 3. Each bbox must tightly enclose its corresponding visible word or text token and must not include adjacent words or unrelated text regions. 4. Preserve the original text exactly without translation, paraphrasing, correction, or completion. 5. Do not add leading or trailing whitespace to text. 6. Include every readable word or text token and exclude non-text visual content. 7. Output strictly valid JSON only. Do not output Markdown, explanations, or code fences. Properly escape quotes, backslashes, and other special characters inside text.

sections.title: 2.2.3 Reference Grounding
sections.content: Reference grounding localizes image content specified by user-provided references. Unlike text spotting, it takes the target references as input and predicts their spatial locations. The output is JSON array ordered by the input references. Each record pairs reference with the bounding box of corresponding visible region, with separate records when reference corresponds to multiple regions. Prompt Locate every visible region corresponding to the requested reference or references in the image. Requested references (JSON array, source order): {references} Return single JSON array in the requested reference order. Each element follows this schema: `{"bbox": [x_min, y_min, x_max, y_max], "reference": "string"}` Rules: 1. Each element must represent exactly one requested reference and one corresponding visible region. If one requested reference corresponds to multiple separate regions, output one element for each bbox and repeat the same reference. 2. The bbox coordinates are integers scaled to [0, 1000). 3. Each bbox must tightly enclose its corresponding referenced entity or region and must not include unrelated content. 4. Copy each reference exactly from the requested-references array without translation, paraphrasing, correction, or completion. Do not output any reference that was not requested. 5. Do not add leading or trailing whitespace to reference. 6. Return bounding boxes only. Do not return points, polygons, masks, explanations, or confidence scores. 7. Every requested reference must appear in at least one output element. 8. Output strictly valid JSON only. Do not output Markdown, explanations, or code fences. Properly escape quotes, backslashes, and other special characters inside reference.

sections.title: 2.2.4 Region OCR
sections.content: Region OCR reads the text within supplied bounding box while retaining the surrounding image as context. The response contains only the text in the requested region. This complements 6 reference grounding: region OCR maps location to text, whereas reference grounding maps supplied reference to its location. Prompt Transcribe all readable text in the specified image region. Directly output the content. Target region: {target_region} Rules: 1. Read only the visible text inside the target region. 2. Preserve the original text exactly without translation, paraphrasing, correction, completion, or omission. 3. Follow the natural human reading order within the target region. 4. Output plain text only. Use spaces and line breaks only where needed to preserve text separation and reading order. 5. Do not output the target region, bounding boxes, coordinates, category labels, Markdown formatting, HTML, JSON, explanations, or code fences.

sections.title: 2.2.5 Formula Recognition
sections.content: Formula recognition transcribes printed or handwritten mathematical expressions into LaTeX, preserving their symbols and spatial structure, including superscripts, subscripts, matrices, and alignments. Each standalone or display expression is enclosed in $$ ... $$, with multiple standalone expressions returned in natural reading order. Prompt Recognize and transcribe every mathematical expression in the image as LaTeX. Directly output the formula content. Rules: 1. Preserve every visible symbol, operator, delimiter, superscript, subscript, accent, matrix row, alignment, and line break without translation, paraphrasing, correction, completion, or omission. 2. Wrap each standalone or display expression as `$$ ... $$`. 3. If multiple standalone expressions are visible, output one `$$ ... $$` block per expression in natural reading order, separated by single line break. 4. Use one decoded backslash for LaTeX command and two decoded backslashes for LaTeX row break. JSON serialization may escape these backslashes on disk, but the decoded target must retain valid LaTeX semantics. 5. Output formula content only. Do not output prose, explanations, translations, Markdown code fences, HTML, document-level table markup, or JSON.

sections.title: 2.2.6 Chart Parsing
sections.content: Chart parsing recovers chart metadata and data values as structured JSON, preserving the organization of series and categories. The output follows fixed schema with title, source, x_title, y_title, and values. Scalar data values are serialized as strings, and unavailable metadata is represented by the literal string "None". For dual-axis charts, y_title may contain two titles in visual order. Prompt Parse all key information in the chart and output one valid JSON object using exactly this top-level schema: {"title":"","source":"","x_title":"","y_title":"","values":{}} Rules: 1. Preserve visible title, source, axis titles, series or category labels, x-axis labels, and values without explanation or inference. 7 Prompt (continued) 2. Use the literal string "None" when the chart has no visible value for title, source, or an axis title. For dual-axis chart, `y_title` may be an array of two strings in visual order; otherwise it must be one string. 3. `values` must be non-empty object. Preserve the chart hierarchy and encode every scalar data value as JSON string. An empty series name may be represented by the key "" when the chart has no visible series label. 4. Output JSON only. Do not output Python syntax, Markdown fences, comments, prose, or extra keys.

sections.title: 2.2.7 Text Translation
sections.content: Text translation renders the readable text within specified image region in target language. It returns only the translated text, preserving the source meaning, names, numbers, symbols, and line order. Prompt Translate all readable text in the specified image region into {target_language}. Directly output the translated content. Target region: {target_region} Rules: 1. Translate only the visible text inside the target region. 2. Preserve the original meaning, names, numbers, symbols, and line order. Do not add explanations, corrections, or omitted context. 3. Keep content that should not be translated unchanged. 4. Output plain translated text only. Use spaces and line breaks only where needed to preserve the source separation. 5. Do not output the source text, language labels, bounding boxes, Markdown, JSON, or code fences. 2.2.

sections.title: Image Classification
sections.content: Image classification assigns an input image to one of the user-provided candidate categories. The candidate set defines the label space, and the model returns single label exactly as supplied. Prompt Classify {target description} in the image. Select exactly one label from the candidate list. Candidate labels: {candidate_labels} Directly output the selected label exactly as written. Do not output explanations, punctuation, JSON, Markdown, or any other text.

sections.title: 2.2.9 Visual Question Answering
sections.content: Visual question answering (VQA) answers natural-language questions by reading and reasoning over image content. It covers text-centric questions about documents, scene text, interfaces, and handwritten content, together with problems involving diagrams, mathematics, science, and visual reasoning. Questions may be open-ended or include answer choices. The prompt requests reasoning followed by final answer enclosed in boxed{}. Prompt {question} Please reason step by step, and put your final answer within boxed{}.

sections.title: 2.2.10 Position-Aware Visual Question Answering
sections.content: Position-aware VQA combines question answering with localization of the answer text in the image. Unlike reference grounding, the target text is not specified in advance but must be identified from the question and image. The output is JSON object with answer and bbox fields. Here, bbox is string in the form "(x1,y1,x2,y2)", encoding the normalized coordinates of tight box around the answer text, rather than the numeric array used by text spotting. Prompt {question} Output the answer with 'answer' and 'bbox'. 'bbox' refers to the bounding box position of the 'answer' content in the image. The output format is "answer:gt, bbox:(x1,y1,x2,y2)", where the bbox is the coordinates of the top-left corner and the bottom-right corners. The 'bbox' should be normalized coordinates ranging from 0 to 1000 by the image width and height. Your answer should be in the JSON format: { "answer": "..", "bbox": "(x1,y1,x2,y2)" # The answer # The bounding box position of the 'answer' }

sections.title: 2.3 Key Information Extraction
sections.content: Key information extraction (KIE) extracts information from an input image and organizes it into structured records. OvisOCR3 supports open extraction, specified-field extraction, and schema-based extraction, which differ in how the target fields and output structure are specified. All three modes request JSON-only output, with field values preserved as written in the image. Empty or missing values are represented by empty strings. Open and specified-field extraction use arrays for repeated values, while schema-based extraction follows the supplied JSON structure.

sections.title: 2.3.1 Open Extraction
sections.content: Open extraction identifies key-value pairs in an input image without predefined field list or output schema. The model determines both the output keys and the organization of the resulting JSON record. Prompt Extract all key-value pairs from the image and return them as JSON object. Keep the values exactly as shown, use empty strings for empty values, and use arrays for repeated values. Output JSON only.

sections.title: 2.3.2 Specified-Field Extraction
sections.content: Specified-field extraction takes user-provided JSON array of field names, such as "company", "date", and "total". The model returns JSON object containing exactly these keys, with values extracted from the image and empty strings for missing fields. Prompt Extract the values for the following keys from the image: {keys_json}. Return JSON object using exactly these keys. Keep the values exactly as shown, use empty strings for missing values, and use arrays for repeated values. Output JSON only.

sections.title: 2.3.3 Schema-Based Extraction
sections.content: Schema-based extraction specifies both the target fields and their organization through userprovided JSON template. Empty strings serve as value placeholders, while nested objects and arrays define the output structure. For example, receipt template can group each items name, quantity, and price within an array element and place payment totals in separate object. Prompt Extract the information from the image using exactly this JSON schema: {schema_json} Keep the values exactly as shown and use empty strings for missing values. Output JSON only.

sections.title: 2.4 Document Figure Captioning
sections.content:
Document figure captioning jointly localizes and describes visual regions in document page, including photographs, illustrations, charts, and flowcharts. Given the full-page image, OvisOCR3 returns JSON array of page regions in reading order, using the same bbox, category, and content fields as structured document parsing. For visual regions, the content field contains an English caption of no more than 100 words enclosed in ..., preserving visible labels in their original language when needed and replacing the image references used in structured parsing. For flowcharts, Mermaid representation of their nodes and connections may follow within .... Text, formulas, and tables retain their Markdown, LaTeX, and HTML representations, respectively. Prompt Analyze the document structure and extract text content. Return single JSON array in natural reading order. Each element follows this schema: `{"bbox": [x_min, y_min, x_max, y_max], "category": "string", "content": "string"}` Rules: 1. The bbox coordinates are integers scaled to [0, 1000). 2. The category is exactly one of: ["abstract", "algorithm", "aside_text", "chart", "content", "display_formula", "doc_title", "figure_title", "footer", "footer_image", "footnote", "formula_number", "header", "header_image", "image", "inline_formula", "number", "paragraph_title", "reference_content", "seal", "table", "text", "vertical_text", "vision_footnote"]. 3. The content formatting depends on category: - For "footer_image", "header_image", "image", or "chart": - Always provide concise English caption of no more than 100 words inside `...`, preserving visible labels in their original language when needed. - For flowchart, valid Mermaid representation may follow the caption inside `...`. - For "display_formula" or "inline_formula": write in LaTeX. - For "table": write as standard HTML `...
`. - Otherwise: write in Markdown. 4. Output must be strictly valid JSON. Properly escape quotes and special characters inside content.

sections.title: 2.5 Cross-Page Table Reconstruction
sections.content: Cross-page table reconstruction recovers complete tables from fragments distributed across consecutive pages, requiring both continuation detection and reconstruction of cell content and structure. OvisOCR3 performs page parsing and cross-page reconstruction with the same model.

sections.title: 2.5.1 Pairwise Table Reconstruction
sections.content:
We use two-stage procedure (Figure 2). First, OvisOCR3 parses each page independently into Markdown, with tables represented in HTML. Second, the same model takes two adjacent page images and their parsed representations to identify cross-page continuations and reconstruct each continued table. The output is JSON array whose records contain the page indices within the input pair (source_pages) and the reconstructed HTML table (html). If no continuation is detected, the model returns an explicit no-continuation result. Prompt Find and reconstruct every table whose content continues across two or more consecutive input pages. Return only one JSON array. Each cross-page table is one object with exactly these fields: source_pages and html. source_pages contains the input-local 1-based pages of that table. html contains one complete HTML ...
. If no cross-page table exists, return [{"source_pages":[],"html":"No cross-page table exists between these pages."}]. Preserve figures inside cross-page tables as ; page_N is 1-based. Return no explanation or code fence. Figure 2: Two-stage cross-page table reconstruction with shared model. Page-level parsing produces Markdown with HTML tables; reconstruction uses these representations together with adjacent page images to identify continuations and recover complete tables.

sections.title: 2.5.2 Recursive Reconstruction
sections.content: For tables spanning more than two pages, we apply pairwise reconstruction recursively within contiguous sequences of pages containing detected tables (Figure 3). We process adjacent pairs from the end of each sequence toward its beginning. After each merge, the reconstructed table is written back to the earlier pages Markdown, which is then re-rendered before that page is paired with its predecessor. Each step uses two page images and their current parsed representations, allowing recovered content to accumulate across multiple pages while retaining the pairwise input format. 11 Figure 3: Recursive reconstruction of table spanning three pages. After merging the fragments on pages 2 and 3, the updated Markdown for page 2 is re-rendered and paired with page 1. Colors denote the source pages of the table fragments. Each step uses two page images and their current parsed representations.

sections.title: 3 Training
sections.content: The training recipe of OvisOCR3 builds on the staged learning paradigm of OvisOCR2 [4], extending its use of supervised learning, on-policy distillation, and model fusion to unified multi-domain model. The central objective is to develop and jointly refine five complementary capabilities: document parsing, general OCR, key information extraction, document figure captioning, and cross-page table reconstruction. These tasks share foundation in text recognition and document structure understanding, but place different emphasis on content reconstruction, field extraction, image-text association, and cross-page structure reconstruction. We therefore adopt staged training process that first builds general capabilities, then integrates domain expertise and jointly refines the model. We organize training into four stages: continued pretraining builds common foundation for the five domains; domain-balanced mid-training rebalances supervision across tasks; multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) transfers domain-specific expertise into shared student; and mixed-task reinforcement learning (MixRL) jointly refines this student with domain-specific rewards.

sections.title: 3.1 Stage 1: Continued Pretraining
sections.content: We initialize OvisOCR3 from Qwen3.5-0.8B [5] and continue training on broad mixture of visual-text tasks. The vision encoder, multimodal connector, and language model are updated jointly. Training examples retain their task-specific instructions and target representations, allowing the same autoregressive model to learn short text answers, structured extractions, captions, and long-form reconstructions. This stage provides common foundation for the five domains before more targeted balancing and post-training. 12 The Stage 1 mixture contains approximately 72 million sampled training examples. Real and synthetic data span diverse document genres, languages, layouts, and acquisition conditions. Document parsing covers textbooks, reports, news, and handwritten notes, together with synthetic layouts, multilingual pages, and photographed or degraded documents. General OCR includes printed and handwritten text recognition, mathematical expressions, chart and document question answering, text translation, and grounding. Key information extraction covers forms, receipts, invoices, and medical documents with both schema-guided and openended extraction targets. Document figure captioning includes figures in real documents and flowcharts, while cross-page table reconstruction includes multi-page tables and positive and negative examples of cross-page relations. Document parsing and general OCR account for approximately 57% and 29% of the sampling budget, respectively, with the remaining budget allocated to the other three domains. We use next-token prediction over reference responses, averaging the loss over supervised response tokens. Sequence packing improves training utilization while preserving the boundaries of individual examples.

sections.title: 3.2 Stage 2: Domain-Balanced Mid-Training
sections.content: Starting from Stage 1, we rebalance the supervised mixture across the five domains. This is particularly important for unified model: datasets vary substantially in size, while an individual example may range from few extracted fields to lengthy structured response. The Stage 2 mixture contains approximately 8.8 million sampled examples, with each domain contributing about 1623% of the sample budget. It retains the five-domain coverage while incorporating challenging cases such as multilingual photographed pages, small or densely arranged figures, extraction targets with empty fields, and hard negative cross-page relations. However, more balanced sample counts do not imply balanced supervision at the token level. General OCR contributes approximately 22.8% of examples but only 5.2% of supervised response tokens; key information extraction contributes 16.1% of examples but only 2.5% of those tokens. The longer responses in document parsing, figure captioning, and cross-page table reconstruction therefore still dominate the supervised token budget. We train two branches with token-level and sample-level loss normalization. Let index the valid examples in training batch, xi and yi denote the input and reference response, and Si contain supervised response positions. The token-level loss is: Ltoken(θ) = iB tSi log pθ(yi,t xi, yi,<t) iB Si . (1) Here, pθ is the models next-token distribution with parameters θ, and yi,t and yi,<t denote the current token and its preceding response prefix. The sample-level loss averages each examples token loss: Lsample(θ) = 1 iB 1 Si log pθ(yi,t xi, yi,<t). sections.title: 3.3 Stage 3: Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation
sections.content: We train five domain-specific 4B teachers, one for each domain. Each teacher is initialized from Qwen3.5-4B [6] and undergoes supervised fine-tuning on its corresponding domain, followed by reinforcement learning with domain-specific rewards. Following on-policy distillation (OPD) [7] and the recipe of OvisOCR2 [4], we distill these teachers into single 0.8B student initialized from the merged Stage 2 model. For an input xi from domain di, the student generates response yi, and the corresponding teacher qdi provides token-level supervision conditioned on the same input and student-generated prefix. Each example is supervised only by its domain teacher, while all domains update the shared student. Our MOPD experiments compare two implementations: policy-gradient optimization and top-K distillation. The policy-gradient implementation uses the teacherstudent log-probability difference on each sampled token as feedback for clipped policy-gradient objective [8]. Top-K distillation [9] instead directly matches the teacher and student distributions over multiple In our experiments, top-K distillation candidate tokens at each student-generated prefix. achieves better overall performance, particularly on document parsing and general OCR tasks. Relative preferences over multiple candidates may help the capacity-constrained 0.8B student better absorb teacher knowledge for coordinated text and structure generation. We therefore adopt this implementation for Stage 3. For top-K distillation, let pθ,i,t and qdi,i,t denote the student and teacher distributions at response position t, renormalized over the rollout students top-K tokens. This support remains fixed during each update. sections.title: 3.4 Stage 4: Mixed-Task Reinforcement Learning
sections.content: After teacher-guided capability integration, MixRL jointly optimizes the model across the five domains using task-specific rewards and domain-balanced input mixture. Domain-specific rewards. MixRL brings diverse tasks into common optimization process while preserving the criteria that define success in each domain. For example, text recognition can be assessed directly against reference transcription, whereas cross-page table reconstruction requires correct table associations before reconstruction quality can be evaluated. Domainspecific rewards encode these distinctions, allowing joint optimization to respect both output fidelity and task-specific structural dependencies: Document parsing. The reward jointly measures text fidelity, table structure and content, and the visual consistency of mathematical expressions. Text is scored by one minus normalized edit distance [10], tables by Tree-Edit-Distance-based Similarity (TEDS) [11], and formulas by Character Detection Matching (CDM) [12] on their rendered representations. Scores are aggregated and normalized over the components present in the reference document, encouraging accurate transcription together with faithful table topology and mathematical notation. General OCR. Rewards target recognition accuracy, answer correctness, or spatial alignment according to the subtask. Text recognition combines edit similarity with exact matching to reward both partial improvements and fully correct transcriptions. Question 14 answering uses answer-type-aware matching for text, numeric values, and categorical answers. Localization uses one-to-one matching with overlap-based scores and duplicateprediction penalties; text spotting additionally combines hard matching scores with continuous IoU feedback. Formula and table recognition use CDM and TEDS, respectively, to assess their content and structure. Key information extraction. Field-value matching forms the main reward component, combined with field-type and list-structure consistency and modulated by field-path coverage. This design evaluates both which fields are extracted and whether their values are correct, rather than rewarding correct schema alone. Additional penalties target incorrect filling of empty fields, omission of nonempty fields, values assigned to the wrong fields, and excessively long extractions. Together, these terms encourage accurate extraction while distinguishing content that should be retained, left empty, or excluded. Document figure captioning. The reward focuses on identifying and spatially grounding the figures to be described, using weighted combination of figure-matching F1 and geometric IoU credit. F1 penalizes both missed and spurious detections, while the geometric term provides graded feedback for imperfect localization. Their combination encourages complete figure identification and accurate spatial extent, including localization improvements below the hard matching threshold. Cross-page table reconstruction. We distinguish relation identification from reconstruction quality. Relation-oriented examples use F1 to penalize both missed and incorrect cross-page associations. Reconstruction-oriented examples follow relation-first reward: TEDS evaluates the merged tables structure and content only when all candidate responses in the group correctly identify the cross-page relations; otherwise, the reward reflects relation correctness. For page-level reconstruction, the quality score also incorporates F1 over non-cross-page content to discourage omissions outside the reconstructed table. Joint policy optimization. We use group-relative policy optimization (GRPO) [13] to jointly optimize the shared model with domain-specific rewards. Advantages are normalized within each response group, allowing heterogeneous reward signals to guide unified policy. Response-level advantages guide token generation through clipped policy objective. An independent KL regularizer constrains policy drift, balancing task improvement with training stability.

sections.title: 4.4 Document Figure Captioning
sections.content: To evaluate document figure captioning, we introduce DocFigCapBench, an in-house benchmark built from PureDocBench, MDPBench, and OmniDocBench. We randomly sampled candidate pages from these sources, then annotated and reviewed them. The final benchmark contains 182 pages with 372 figure targets and 161 ignored visual regions. Annotators marked information-bearing figures using the original pages and candidate locations from document parsers, while designating decorative graphics and header or footer visuals as ignored regions. Reference captions were drafted by VLM and checked against the images for factual errors, omissions, and hallucinations (Figure 4). For multi-image figures, both the enclosing group and its individual members were annotated (Figure 5), allowing evaluation to accept either group-level or member-level detections. Using these annotations, we evaluate figure detection with Localization F1 and end-to-end figure captioning with Caption Score. For localization, predictions are matched to figure targets at an IoU threshold of 0.5. group-level prediction for multi-image figure must additionally cover at least 80% of each member, while member-level matches receive credit proportional to the fraction of members detected. Unmatched predictions are excluded from scoring if their IoU with an ignored region is at least 0.3 or at least 80% of their area falls within it. We compute F1 as the harmonic mean of precision and recall on each page, then average it across all 182 pages and report the result as percentage. Pages without figure targets receive full credit if they have no counted predictions, and zero otherwise. For Caption Score, Qwen3.8-Max [25] scores captions for matched figures on 010 scale, using the image as the basis for judgment and the reference caption as checklist. Missed figures and empty captions receive zero. For groups matched through their members, we average all member scores, including zeros for missed members. Figure scores are then averaged within each page and across the 177 pages containing figure targets. OvisOCR3 and the general VLM baselines use the same full-page prompt, which requests English captions of no more than 100 words, preserves visible labels in their original language when needed, and permits Mermaid representations for flowcharts. Invalid outputs are treated as empty predictions and remain in the evaluation denominators, including eight formatfailed pages from Qwen3.7-Plus. Specialized OCR baselines use their native document-parsing workflows. sections.title: 4.5 Cross-Page Table Reconstruction
sections.content: We evaluate cross-page table reconstruction on MPDocBench-Parse [3] and CrossTabBench. MPDocBench-Parse covers 15 document types in English and Chinese and includes truncatedtable reconstruction task. To further assess continuation detection and reconstruction across varied layouts, we introduce CrossTabBench, an in-house benchmark drawn from multilingual documents with both vertical continuations and horizontal stitching. It contains 890 consecutivepage pairs comprising 1,780 images: 491 pairs require table reconstruction, while the remaining 399 require no cross-page merge. Figure 6 illustrates an annotated example. On CrossTabBench, we assess continuation detection with Relation F1 and reconstruction quality with Reconstruction TEDS. Relation F1 is the harmonic mean of precision and recall computed over all 890 page pairs, with false merges counted as false positives and missed continuations as false negatives. Missing or malformed outputs count as incorrect decisions. Evaluation operates at the page-pair level, rather than on individual cells or table fragments. Reconstruction TEDS measures how accurately the reconstructed tables preserve structure and cell text. For each positive case with valid output and correct continuation decision, we normalize the reference and predicted HTML tables and find the one-to-one matching that maximizes their total TEDS. Unmatched reference tables receive zero, as do cases with invalid outputs or incorrect continuation decisions. Scores are summed and divided by the fixed total of 491 reference tables, so missed continuations remain in the denominator. The 399 negative pairs affect Relation F1 but not Reconstruction TEDS. On MPDocBench-Parse, we follow the benchmarks truncated-table TEDS protocol [3], which does not impose this explicit continuation-decision gate. All metrics are reported on 0100 scale. OvisOCR3 and the general VLM baseline follow the same two-stage procedure: each model first parses the pages, then reconstructs cross-page tables using the page images and its own parsed representations. Specialized parsers use their provided inference pipelines. For document-level 23 Figure 6: An annotated two-page example from CrossTabBench. Red boxes mark fragments of the same table, with enlarged views below the source pages. The ground-truth reconstruction on the right preserves merged cells and numerical values. evaluation, we apply the recursive reconstruction procedure described in Section 2.5, with candidate page sequences determined from model predictions rather than reference annotations. sections.title: 5 Conclusion
sections.content: In this report, we present OvisOCR3, compact 0.8B model that unifies document parsing, general OCR, key information extraction, document figure captioning, and cross-page table reconstruction. We train the model on real and synthetic data using four-stage recipe comprising 24 continued pretraining, domain-balanced mid-training, multi-teacher on-policy distillation, and mixed-task reinforcement learning. Evaluated on public and in-house benchmarks, OvisOCR3 achieves leading results across broad range of OCR tasks, outperforming both general-purpose vision-language models and specialized OCR models on multiple benchmarks.
